title: What is Private Equity?
subtitle: Investing in unlisted companies to create value
openingQuestion: What is the main difference between PE and VC?
openingOptions: PE simply uses more debt, but both target the same stage
PE buys mature companies via LBO; VC funds early startups
PE only invests in real estate and physical infrastructure
PE is just a bigger version of VC, with the same strategy
explanation: Private equity buys stakes in unlisted companies, usually buying outright to take control. The core difference from venture capital lies in the stage and how returns are generated: buyout funds target mature businesses with stable cash flow and use leverage, while venture funds put in pure equity capital into young businesses and accept that most investments will be lost.

diagram.label: PE: buy a mature company, restructure it
Both exit via IPO or sale

realWorldExample.company: KKR, Blackstone, and major buyout deals
realWorldExample.description: Leading Private Equity funds like KKR or Blackstone typically buy mature companies, optimize operations and capital structure over 5-7 years, then exit via IPO or sale to another fund - a business model completely different from venture capital funds that put money into early-stage startups.

quiz.question: How does PE exit?
options: Hold forever - PE funds have no time limit so exiting isn't necessary
Pay a steady annual dividend to investors instead of having to sell the company to anyone
Let the company go bankrupt to wipe out debt, then buy the assets back cheap
IPO, sell to a strategic buyer, or sell to another PE fund - usually after 5-7 years
quiz.explanation: PE funds typically have a 10-year term (5-7 years holding + 2-3 years raising + exiting). Exit options: IPO (highest liquidity), strategic sale (usually the highest price due to synergy), secondary buyout (sold to another PE fund). Each exit route offers a different degree of liquidity.

quiz.question: Why does an individual investor wanting exposure to Private Equity returns usually face much greater difficulty than investing in ordinary listed shares?
options: Very high minimum capital and multi-year lock-ups, reserved for institutions
Anyone can invest in PE as easily as buying a stock, just by opening an account
Because PE always returns lower profit than listed shares so few bother
Because PE funds are legally barred from accepting domestic investors
quiz.explanation: Private Equity has high barriers to entry (large minimum capital, low liquidity, long lock-up periods) - which is why PE's potentially higher returns are usually reserved for large institutional investors (pension funds, sovereign wealth funds) and ultra-wealthy individuals, not ordinary public investors.

quiz.question: What is the core difference between PE and VC?
options: PE invests with equity capital, VC invests mainly with borrowed debt
PE buys mature companies with cash flow, VC funds startups
PE only operates in developed markets, VC operates everywhere
PE takes minority stakes, VC always takes control
quiz.explanation: PE buys control of a company that already has stable cash flow and then restructures it, usually using significant leverage. VC buys minority stakes in businesses without profits yet and accepts that most will be lost entirely.

quiz.question: Why do PE funds usually use large debt leverage when buying a company?
options: Because the target company usually doesn't have enough cash to operate
Because banks require a minimum debt ratio in every deal they underwrite
Because debt amplifies the return on the equity capital put in
Because interest expense helps lower the purchase price of the company
quiz.explanation: Putting in 30 units of equity and borrowing 70 to buy an asset worth 100; if the asset rises to 130, the equity slice doubles. This mechanism also runs in reverse, so PE only uses it with companies whose cash flow is solid enough to service the debt.

quiz.question: Why is it hard for individual investors to access PE?
options: Because PE returns are lower so it doesn't attract individuals
Because regulations ban individuals from investing in private equity funds
Because PE funds only accept capital from investors in the same country
Because minimum capital is very large and money is locked up for years
quiz.explanation: Commitments are usually measured in millions of dollars, and the money is locked up for 7-10 years without being able to withdraw. These are two real barriers, quite unlike listed shares that trade freely for a few million dong.

keyTakeaways: PE: buy mature companies, restructure them, exit after 5-7 years
PE vs VC: PE = mature + LBO; VC = startup + equity
Exit: IPO, strategic sale, or secondary buyout

practicePrompt.question: A fund buys a retail chain that has operated for 20 years, with stable cash flow but poorly run operations. The fund uses debt leverage, replaces management, cuts costs, and optimizes operations over 6 years, then sells or IPOs the company at a much higher price. Which type of fund does this investment model characterize?
options: This is characteristic of Venture Capital, because the fund is investing in a company to create growth value
PE buys mature companies that already have steady cash flow, restructures them, then exits after five to seven years
This is characteristic of a bond fund, because it focuses on the target company's stable cash flow
This is a direct IPO transaction, because the company is sold to the market after being restructured
practicePrompt.explanation: PE: buy mature companies, restructure them, exit after 5-7 years. Unlike VC, which targets high-risk early-stage startups, Private Equity targets already-mature companies with stable cash flow - using debt leverage and operational improvement to increase value before exiting via sale or IPO.

summary.keyIdea: PE: buy mature companies, restructure them, exit after 5-7 years
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: PE vs VC: PE = mature + LBO; VC = startup + equity

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up a PE or VC fund operating in Vietnam, and check what stage they publicly say they invest in (early-stage startups or already-mature companies) to clearly tell PE apart from VC.
application.secondary: This helps you read corporate fundraising news more accurately.

sections.text: Private Equity (PE) and Venture Capital (VC) are often lumped together, but they are actually two clearly distinct investment models: PE targets already-mature companies to restructure and optimize operations, while VC targets early-stage startups to bet on breakthrough growth.
What PE does and how it exits

Buyout PE funds like KKR or Blackstone buy mature companies that already have stable cash flow, then restructure operations and improve efficiency over roughly 5-7 years, then exit via one of three routes: IPO (highest liquidity), sale to a strategic buyer (usually the highest price thanks to strategic synergy), or sale to another PE fund (secondary buyout). A PE fund's term typically runs 10 years: roughly 5-7 years of holding plus 2-3 years of raising and exiting.
Why PE is hard for individual investors to access

Unlike listed shares that can be freely bought and sold at any time with a small amount of capital, PE funds usually require a very large minimum investment (millions of dollars) and lock up capital for many years, reserved for institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals (accredited investors). This is why PE's potentially higher returns are usually reserved for large institutional investors like pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and ultra-wealthy individuals - not ordinary public investors.

left.label: Private Equity
left.text: Buys mature companies, uses LBO (large debt leverage), funds usually over $1 billion, aims to improve operations and capital structure.

right.label: Venture Capital
right.text: Invests in early-stage startups (seed through Series A-D), uses pure equity with no debt leverage, funds usually $100-500 million, bets on breakthrough growth following the power law.

items: PE: buy mature companies, restructure them, exit after 5-7 years via IPO/strategic sale/secondary buyout
VC: fund early-stage startups, accept high risk following the power law
Barriers to PE access: large minimum capital, low liquidity, multi-year lock-ups

lines: PE and VC both invest 'off the stock exchange', but they bet on two completely different stages of a company's life cycle.
